newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian police club protesters to break blockade.
newsitem.headline: Serbian police club protesters to break blockade.

text.p: Serbian security police clubbed opposition protesters seated across a highway on Thursday to break a blockade of the city of Kragujevac and seven people were seriously injured, witnesses said.

They said police left one woman lying in a pool of blood before an ambulance came while an opposition member of the Yugoslav federal parliament, Zoran Simonovic, suffered a severe brain concussion and was admitted to hospital.

Fifteen people had light injuries, said Sveta Nikolic, vice-president of the new moderate coalition administration in Kragujevac that took office after defeating long-entrenched leftists in regional elections two months ago.
Police also temporarily detained two international news agency cameramen and seized their film.

Supporters of the new Zajedno (Together) municipal government had sealed off routes to Kragujevac after outgoing Socialist Party (SPS) authorities refused to surrender the regional radio and television centre (RTK).

Angry Zajedno demonstrators massed outside RTK for a second day running after police "occupied" it to preserve SPS control. The new Zajedno city government cut off the building's utility supplies to ratchet up pressure on the SPS.

The Zajedno protesters on the highway were assaulted by 100 baton-wielding security police sent by the Socialist central government in Belgrade to unblock Kragujevac, an industrial city of 200,000 in central Serbia.
Violence has been rare in more than two months of pro-democracy demonstrations across Serbia.

But the incident was likely to aggravate the confrontation between Zajedno and President Slobodan Milosevic's authoritarian Socialists over their annulment of municipal elections in 14 cities won by the opposition coalition.

Zajedno has staged mass street protests across Serbia for almost 10 weeks in a bid to restore their election victories and force Milosevic to undertake democratic reform in federal Yugoslavia, including a liberalisation of the media.
Zajedno activists briefly blocked a few other roads in Serbia on Thursday, resulting in several arrests and clashes with riot police, independent local media reported.
Police detained five opposition leaders in the eastern town of Smederevo for three hours, Belgrade radio B-92 said.

Kragujevac was not one of 14 cities where voting was nullified. Zajedno won Kragujevac without the allegations of "irregularities" that led to annulments elsewhere, but SPS diehards refused to surrender influential regional airwaves.
About 200 security police entered the RTK building on Wednesday morning to preserve SPS control while the party tried to stall a handover by filing court action.
Some 10,000 supporters of Zajedno besieged the building on Wednesday, dispersing overnight.

Thousands massed in front of the complex again on Thursday as the new town authorities and officials of Serbian state television (RTS) held talks inside. They ended in mid-evening without agreement but were to resume on Friday.
Zajedno said it had offered to withdraw the protesters if two officials it has nominated to manage RTK as a non-partisan station were allowed to take over pending a final court ruling.
"If this proposal is not accepted I'm afraid we may not be able to control the situation, which is in turmoil," said Borivoje Radic, a senior Zajedno official in Kragujevac.

In Belgrade, 70,000 Zajedno demonstrators rallied without incident in Republic Square and were addressed by former East German dissidents who led mass protests that brought down that country's Stalinist regime peacefully in 1989.
"I want to tell you something we learnt and will not forget -- that courage, numbers and audacity can move mountains," said Marianne Birthler, now a Greens legislator in united Germany.
